turn_text: Is rural broadband now considered still a luxury? Or is this more of an essential service, much like telecommunications and even electricity from years ago?

That's not doable for all of rural America. And I think it's much better if we just had actual broadband to the farm and to the towns. And so things have changed and business has changed. And that's what I'm so struck by 10 years ago. People were just talking about getting any access. Senator Soon. the head of the Commerce Committee in which I serve and I joined together. With regard to your legislation in Cuba, is that the complete elimination of the embargo or is it rolling it back to provide a better opportunity for agriculture?

Well, this is, there are provisions, there are, I've been on bill before, that just focus on agriculture and I still am. But actually, this actually lists the embargo because I've become convinced if we just lift the travel ban, which is the conventional wisdom that's what we'll do first. And we may, I'm on that bill as well. But suddenly we're going to have five million Americans a year traveling just 90 miles to an island of 11 million people. And they can do it by boat, they can do it by plane. There's going to be this influx of tourism. And if we're not careful and we don't list the embargo to allow ag products in and construction and ag machinery and other things, Pretty soon, these Americans are going to be sleeping in Spanish hotels in Cuba and eating Chinese food, because we're going to lose out on this market. And I have been at the port, the new part there, Mario, and it's a big, big port, and we want Americans' ships and Americans' bits to be landing in that port. And right now, just to give you an example, that port was financed by South Americans and Brazilians And the computer system is Chinese, and almost all these other ports have American computer systems. But they're not allowed to do that. And I just don't think that's good for the people, and it's not good for ad country, and it's not good for America. And so our hope is that by lifting the whole embargo, we would be in the best place in terms of doing business. One interesting agriculture perspective, having been there now with Secretary Bill Seck with the President and meeting with that group there, is there's a real opportunity for organic agriculture in Cuba because, and I know some of our domestic providers sometimes concerned about the competition. Well, as you know, we have a big organic market here and we can make about 1% of it, about 20% of what we need, about 5% of the needs are organic right now. And so there's a big market there for organic produce where they could split scale, not just little farms with big scale, start doing organic because of the land quality and all kinds of things and get certified right away. So that's one of the things that Bill Beck is pushing for, and I don't think that would directly be competitive nearly as much because we need more organic. So that was an interesting thing that I learned over there. The other one, and I'll end with this on Cuba, is just be it. amazing change that we've seen in the attitude of the American people and the Cuban people with us on the plane last summer where we opened the embassy with Secretary Kerry with three Marines. Mike Berry and I think the other guy's name was Joe or something like that. And they had come with us because they were the ones that were given a really difficult job 50 some years ago of taking the American flag down over the embassy when we closed it. to jeering crowds, and one of them turned to the crowds and said, we will return. 50 some years later, the old Marines were back and they handed a new flag to three young Marines who hoisted up over the embassy. And it just gives you that sense that things can change and our relations with other countries can change. We see this as a real opportunity.
